mcq.section: Concurrency, Parallelism, and the Units of Execution
mcq.prompt: What distinguishes concurrency from parallelism?
choices: Concurrency requires multiple cores; parallelism does not
They are two names for the same property, one from the language and one from the hardware
Concurrency structures a program as independently progressing activities; parallelism executes activities physically at the same time
Concurrency describes processes; parallelism describes threads
mcq.explain: Concurrency is a structuring property — a concurrent program can interleave its activities on a single core. Parallelism is a physical property and needs multiple processing resources. Treating them as synonyms is the mistake that leads people to expect a speedup from adding threads on a one-core machine, where the structure is unchanged but no work overlaps.

mcq.section: Concurrency, Parallelism, and the Units of Execution
mcq.prompt: A task suspends inside a thread pool and is later resumed. What does that imply for `thread_local` state?
choices: The task resumes on the worker that started it, so thread-local state follows the task
The task may resume on a different worker, so thread-local state belongs to the execution thread, not to the logical request
Tasks always own a thread for their lifetime, so the question does not arise
The pool copies thread-local state to the new worker when a task migrates
mcq.explain: A task is an application-level unit of work assigned to a thread; a pool can run thousands of tasks on a fixed set of workers and a resumed task may land on a different one. Nothing copies thread-local state across that boundary, so request-scoped data stored in TLS silently belongs to whichever worker happens to be running. Storing request semantics in TLS is only safe when tasks are deliberately pinned.

mcq.prompt: A `std::thread` object is destroyed while it is still joinable. What happens?
choices: It joins automatically, waiting for the thread to finish
It detaches automatically and the thread runs on
The behaviour is undefined
It calls std::terminate
mcq.explain: The destructor of a joinable std::thread calls std::terminate — a deliberate design choice, because neither silently joining (an unexpected blocking wait) nor silently detaching (an unexpected lifetime escape) is safe to guess. This is not undefined behaviour: it is a defined, loud failure. std::jthread exists precisely so that the automatic answer can be 'request stop, then join'.

mcq.prompt: What does the destructor of `std::jthread` do?
choices: It requests a cooperative stop through its stop source, then joins
It joins first, then requests stop for any other threads sharing the token
It detaches the thread so the destructor never blocks
It forcibly terminates the running thread
mcq.explain: The order matters: requesting stop first gives a cooperating worker the chance to notice and return, and only then does the destructor block in join(). Joining first would deadlock against a worker looping until it is asked to stop. Nothing about jthread is preemptive — a worker that never polls its token still makes the destructor wait indefinitely.

mcq.prompt: A class holds a `std::mutex`, a `std::queue`, and a `std::jthread` worker that uses both. Where should the jthread member be declared?
choices: First, so the worker is constructed before the state it uses
Anywhere — member destruction order does not affect a jthread
Last, so it is destroyed first and joins while the mutex and queue are still alive
Last, so that it is constructed first and can prime the queue
mcq.explain: Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, so the last-declared member is destroyed first. Declaring the jthread last makes its automatic join run while the mutex and queue it touches are still constructed. Declaring it first inverts that: the queue and mutex are destroyed while a worker may still be using them, which is a use-after-destruction bug the compiler will not diagnose.

mcq.prompt: Passing `counter` directly to a thread whose callable takes `int&` fails to compile; wrapping it as `std::ref(counter)` fixes that. Which problem does `std::ref` NOT solve?
choices: Binding the thread's stored argument to an `int&` parameter
The requirement that `counter` outlive the worker's use of it
Making the argument storable in the thread's internal argument tuple
The decay-copy that would otherwise hand the callable a copy
mcq.explain: std::ref produces a copyable reference_wrapper, which both satisfies the decay-copy requirement and converts back to int& at the call — so it fixes the invocability problem. It says nothing about lifetime. If counter is a local and the thread is detached, or joined after the enclosing scope has already returned, the worker still holds a dangling reference. Reference semantics and lifetime are separate obligations.

mcq.prompt: How many instances does a `thread_local std::mt19937 engine` have, and when is each destroyed?
choices: One per process, destroyed at program exit
One per thread, destroyed when that thread exits
One per call to the enclosing function, destroyed at end of scope
One per thread, all destroyed together at program exit
mcq.explain: A thread_local object has exactly one instance per thread, constructed on first odr-use when dynamic initialization is required and destroyed during that thread's teardown — not at process exit. That per-thread teardown is why thread-local destructors can recreate destruction-order hazards against other thread-local or static objects.

mcq.prompt: Which statement about the cost of thread-local storage is accurate?
choices: Access is always a single fixed offset from a thread register
Dynamic initialization runs once per process, like a namespace-scope static
A large `thread_local` buffer costs the same as one global buffer of the same size
A dynamically initialized thread-local needs a per-thread guard check on access, and a large one multiplies footprint by the number of participating threads
mcq.explain: Both halves matter. The guard check is per thread because the constructor must run once for every thread that reaches the declaration — an expensive constructor is paid N times, not once. And N threads means N copies of the object, so a worst-case-sized scratch buffer silently becomes N worst-case buffers. The fixed-offset access model applies to static TLS in the main executable; dynamic TLS in a shared library may go through a helper such as __tls_get_addr.

mcq.section: Data Races and the Mutex Family
mcq.prompt: Two threads run this concurrently on a single available permit and both return true. Classify the defect.
choices: A data race, because two threads touch the same memory location and one writes
Neither — atomic operations make the sequence correct by construction
A race condition without a data race: every access is race-free, but check-then-act is not one transaction
A data race only if the atomic operations use relaxed ordering
mcq.explain: A data race is specifically the undefined-behaviour case of unsynchronized access, and there is none here — every access goes through std::atomic. The bug is a race condition: an incorrect result produced by an unfortunate interleaving. Both threads observe 1, both subtract, and the permit count goes negative. Making individual operations atomic never makes a compound decision atomic; that needs a single read-modify-write such as a compare-exchange loop.

mcq.section: Data Races and the Mutex Family
mcq.prompt: Two threads each execute `++counter` a million times on a plain `int` with no synchronization. What does the standard say the program does?
choices: It has undefined behaviour — no valid final value is guaranteed
It prints some value between 1,000,000 and 2,000,000, chosen by the interleaving
It prints exactly 2,000,000, because an increment compiles to a single instruction
It is implementation-defined, but always prints a value the hardware actually produced
mcq.explain: The tempting answer is the 'lost updates' story — that you get some plausible number between one and two million. That describes a hardware outcome, not the language rule. A data race is undefined behaviour, so the compiler may hoist the increment out of the loop, keep counter in a register, or assume the race cannot happen; the printed value need not correspond to any interleaving at all. ThreadSanitizer, not reasoning about instructions, is the tool that finds these.

mcq.section: Data Races and the Mutex Family
mcq.prompt: Which mutex lets the same thread acquire it again without deadlocking, and what does reaching for it usually indicate?
choices: std::timed_mutex; that the caller needs a bounded wait
std::recursive_mutex; that the locking boundary is unclear and a public/private split would state it better
std::shared_mutex; that reads dominate writes
std::mutex; relocking from the owning thread is permitted by default
mcq.explain: std::recursive_mutex tracks an owner and a count so the holder may relock. It is legal but usually a symptom: the code cannot tell whether a given function is entered with the lock held. The standard fix is a public function that locks once and private helpers whose names or contracts state that the lock is already held. Relocking a plain std::mutex from the owning thread is undefined behaviour, not a permitted operation.

mcq.section: RAII Lock Wrappers and Multi-Lock Deadlock Avoidance
mcq.prompt: Which lock wrapper can be used with `condition_variable::wait`?
choices: std::lock_guard
std::scoped_lock
std::unique_lock
Any of the three — the condition variable only needs the mutex
mcq.explain: wait() must atomically release the mutex, park, and reacquire before returning, so the wrapper has to track whether it currently owns the mutex and support unlocking and relocking. Only std::unique_lock does. lock_guard and scoped_lock are deliberately minimal: they acquire at construction and release at destruction with no state in between, which is why they compile to less but cannot express a wait.

mcq.section: RAII Lock Wrappers and Multi-Lock Deadlock Avoidance
mcq.prompt: What does `std::scoped_lock lock{from.mutex, to.mutex};` provide over locking the two mutexes one after the other?
choices: It is faster, because it takes both locks in one atomic operation
It orders the mutexes by address, which the standard requires it to do
It converts both mutexes into shared locks so readers are not excluded
It uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm rather than holding one mutex while blocking indefinitely on the next
mcq.explain: Sequential locking creates hold-and-wait: a caller holding `from` and blocking on `to` can deadlock against a caller doing the reverse. scoped_lock avoids that by never waiting indefinitely for the second mutex while retaining the first — conceptually acquire, fail, release, retry. Address ordering is one possible implementation, but the standard specifies the deadlock-avoidance result, not the algorithm, and there is no hardware operation that locks two mutexes at once.

mcq.section: RAII Lock Wrappers and Multi-Lock Deadlock Avoidance
mcq.prompt: Which of these belongs OUTSIDE the critical section?
choices: Formatting the copied state into a log line
Reading the guarded field
Updating the guarded field
Copying the guarded field into a local
mcq.explain: The critical section should cover exactly the guarded state: read it, update it, copy out what later work needs, then release. Formatting allocates and may perform I/O, and allocation acquires allocator-internal locks — so holding an application mutex across it nests unrelated lock hierarchies and stretches the hold time by the allocator's variable work. Copying the field out is the mechanism that makes the formatting safe to do unlocked, so it must stay inside.

mcq.prompt: Why can `std::shared_mutex` be slower than a plain `std::mutex` even when 95% of operations are reads?
choices: Because std::shared_lock silently escalates to an exclusive lock under contention
Because readers must serialize with one another anyway
Because every reader updates shared reader bookkeeping whose cache line bounces between cores, and short read sections never recover that cost
Because the standard mandates writer preference, which stalls arriving readers
mcq.explain: Reader parallelism is not free: recording how many readers are active is itself a shared write, so the count's cache line migrates between cores even though the protected data is only read. If the read section is short, that bookkeeping dominates and a plain mutex — which serializes less machinery — wins. Readers genuinely do not exclude one another, and the standard interface exposes no portable fairness selection at all, so neither reader nor writer preference can be assumed.

mcq.prompt: Which lock types do readers and writers use with `std::shared_mutex`?
choices: std::shared_lock for readers, std::unique_lock for writers
std::unique_lock for readers, std::shared_lock for writers
std::lock_guard for both — the mutex decides which mode to use
std::shared_lock for both; the mutex promotes the writer automatically
mcq.explain: The wrapper, not the mutex, selects the mode: shared_lock calls lock_shared(), unique_lock calls lock(). Nothing infers the intent from the operation, and there is no promotion from shared to exclusive — attempting to build one is a classic deadlock, since two readers can each wait for the other to release before either can upgrade.

mcq.prompt: Why does the canonical wait pass a predicate rather than calling `condition.wait(lock)` on its own?
choices: Because the one-argument wait() does not release the mutex while parked
Because passing a predicate lets the implementation skip the kernel wait entirely
Because notify_one() would otherwise wake every waiter
Because a wait may wake spuriously, and because a notification sent before the wait begins is lost unless durable state records it
mcq.explain: Two independent reasons, and both are about the predicate being a statement about *state*. Spurious wakeups mean returning from wait() proves nothing, so the condition must be rechecked — the two-argument overload is exactly the `while (!pred()) wait(lock);` loop. And because condition variables do not store signals, a notification that arrives before any thread waits is discarded; only durable predicate state records that work is available. Both overloads release the mutex while parked.

mcq.prompt: One thread calls `send_broken()` while no thread is waiting; another thread then calls `receive_broken()`. What happens?
choices: The waiter returns immediately, because the notification was queued for the next waiter
The waiter may sleep forever: condition variables do not store signals, and nothing durable recorded that work was available
The waiter returns immediately, because wait() rechecks the mutex before parking
The program is ill-formed, because wait() requires a predicate
mcq.explain: A condition variable is a parking mechanism, not a message queue. notify_one() with no waiter present wakes nobody and is discarded — there is no counter and no pending-signal state. The receiver then parks with nothing left to wake it. The fix is not a bigger timeout but a durable predicate: set a `ready_` flag under the mutex before notifying, so a consumer that arrives late sees a true predicate and never parks at all. (A spurious wake could still rescue this particular program by accident, which is exactly why it must not be relied on.)

mcq.prompt: When is `notify_all()` required rather than `notify_one()`?
choices: Whenever more than one thread might be waiting on the condition variable
Never — notify_one() is always sufficient and always cheaper
When one state change may enable several waiters, or when different waiters test different predicates on the same condition variable
Only when the notifier still holds the mutex at the point of notification
mcq.explain: notify_one() is correct when one newly available item satisfies exactly one interchangeable consumer — several waiters is fine in that case, since only one can take the item. It breaks down when a single change enables several waiters, or when waiters test different predicates and notify_one() may wake one whose predicate is still false while the one that could proceed stays parked. Waking everyone for a single item is the thundering-herd cost you pay to avoid that.

mcq.prompt: `Config& config() { static Config instance = load_config(); return instance; }` is called concurrently by several threads. What is guaranteed?
choices: Initialization happens exactly once; concurrent callers block until it completes and then observe the initialized object
Each thread initializes its own instance
The behaviour is undefined without an explicit mutex around the static
Initialization is repeated on each thread until every thread has run it once
mcq.explain: A function-local static — a 'magic static' — is required to be initialized exactly once even under concurrent first calls; the implementation inserts a guard that makes the losing threads wait. Adding a mutex around it is redundant, and adding an unsynchronized `bool initialized` beside it reintroduces exactly the data race and partial-publication hazard the guard removes. Note the one escape hatch: if load_config() throws, initialization did not complete and a later call may retry.

mcq.prompt: The callable passed to `std::call_once` throws. What is the state of the `std::once_flag` afterwards?
choices: Set — later calls do nothing, so the object stays half-initialized
Set — later calls rethrow the stored exception
Unset — the exception propagates to that caller, and another call may try again
Undefined — the once_flag must be destroyed and recreated
mcq.explain: call_once completes the flag only when the callable returns normally, so a throwing attempt leaves the flag unset and the exception reaches its caller. That is what makes retry possible and is the same rule magic statics follow. The tempting wrong answer — flag set, object half-initialized — would be the behaviour of a hand-rolled `if (!done) { init(); done = true; }` if `done` were set before the work, which is one more reason not to hand-roll it.

mcq.section: The C++20 Kit: Semaphores, Latches, Barriers, and Atomic Wait
mcq.prompt: Which property distinguishes `std::counting_semaphore` from `std::mutex`?
choices: A semaphore has no thread ownership — one thread may acquire a permit and a different thread may release it
A semaphore never blocks; it returns false when no permit is available
A semaphore is always faster, because it never reaches the kernel
A semaphore integrates with std::lock_guard and std::unique_lock
mcq.explain: The absence of ownership is exactly what makes a semaphore right for signalling and resource slots — the thread that finishes an order can release the permit the submitting thread acquired. It is also why a binary_semaphore is a poor mutex substitute: there is no owner to check, no relocking diagnostic, and no lock-wrapper integration, so a stray release simply invents a permit and quietly breaks the resource bound.

mcq.section: The C++20 Kit: Semaphores, Latches, Barriers, and Atomic Wait
mcq.prompt: What is the difference between `std::latch` and `std::barrier`?
choices: A latch is reusable across phases; a barrier is one-shot
Both are reusable, but only a barrier can run a completion function
Both are one-shot; a barrier merely adds a completion function
A latch is a one-shot countdown that stays open once it reaches zero; a barrier resets for the next phase
mcq.explain: Reusability is the axis. A latch counts down once and, once open, stays open and cannot be reset — right for facts that happen once, like 'all workers are ready'. A barrier is a repeated phase boundary: every participant arrives, an optional completion step runs, and the barrier resets so the next phase can use it. That reset also creates an obligation a latch does not have — every remaining participant must reach every phase, or its peers wait forever.

mcq.section: The C++20 Kit: Semaphores, Latches, Barriers, and Atomic Wait
mcq.prompt: What does `ready.wait(false)` do on a `std::atomic<bool> ready`?
choices: Waits until the value becomes false
Blocks while the atomic still equals false, returning once a store changes it and notification wakes the waiter
Spins for an implementation-defined period and then throws on timeout
Registers a callback to be invoked on the next store to the atomic
mcq.explain: The argument is the value the waiter expects to be *stale*: wait(old) blocks while the atomic still equals old. Reading it as 'wait until it becomes false' is the classic inversion and produces a program that returns instantly and then reads unpublished data. The implementation checks in user space first and can park with futex-shaped machinery, which is why the publisher must call notify_one/notify_all after the store.

mcq.section: Spinning, Parking, and What a Mutex Really Is
mcq.prompt: On an oversubscribed machine, why can a pure spin lock be catastrophic rather than merely wasteful?
choices: Because the atomic exchange in the spin loop is slower than a system call
Because a spinning thread cannot be interrupted by a signal or preempted
Because the spinner can consume the very time slice the descheduled lock holder needs in order to run and release
Because spin locks cannot be used with RAII lock wrappers
mcq.explain: Spinning trades CPU for wake latency, and that trade is fine when the holder is running and will release promptly. When the holder has been descheduled, the spinner burns a full logical core doing nothing while blocking the only thread that can make progress — the waste becomes a livelock-shaped stall rather than a small overhead. A secondary effect compounds it: a tight exchange loop writes the lock's cache line on every attempt, so the waiting itself slows the owner down. Spin-then-park bounds the failure.

mcq.section: Spinning, Parking, and What a Mutex Really Is
mcq.prompt: What does the kernel-side futex wait check before putting the caller to sleep, and why does it matter?
choices: That the futex word still holds the expected value — otherwise unlock already happened and the waiter would sleep through the release
That the calling thread's priority exceeds the current holder's, to avoid inversion
That no other waiter is already queued, so that FIFO order is preserved
That the mutex is not recursive, since recursion would corrupt the wait queue
mcq.explain: There is a window between the user-space code observing a locked word and the thread actually entering the kernel. If unlock lands in that window, the wake finds no waiter, and a naive implementation would then park forever. Passing the expected value into the futex wait closes it: the kernel re-checks under its own lock and returns immediately if the value has changed. This is what keeps the uncontended path in user space — one compare-and-swap to acquire, one store to release, no syscall — while remaining correct under contention.

mcq.prompt: In the chapter's ThreadPool, why is `task()` invoked after the `unique_lock`'s scope has ended?
choices: Because std::function is not safe to invoke while any mutex is held
Because the condition variable requires its mutex to be free during a notify
Because the mutex protects the queue, not execution — running the task under it would serialize the whole pool and let arbitrary user code block submission
Because the task may call submit() itself, and std::mutex is recursive
mcq.explain: The mutex's written invariant is 'this mutex guards the task queue'. Executing user code inside it widens that invariant to cover the entire pool: workers could no longer run concurrently, and a task that blocks would also block every producer trying to submit. That is why the worker moves the callable into a local — transferring ownership before the critical section ends — and only then calls it. std::mutex is emphatically not recursive, which makes the reentrant-submit answer a deadlock rather than a justification.

mcq.prompt: Every task running in a fixed-size pool synchronously waits for the result of another task submitted to the same pool. What is the failure?
choices: Livelock — the workers spin, react to each other, and never complete
Deadlock by starvation — every worker is blocked on work that remains queued behind the blocked workers
Priority inversion — the queued tasks effectively outrank the running ones
A lock convoy — the workers parade one at a time through the queue mutex
mcq.explain: There is no lock cycle here and no CPU burn, which is why 'deadlock' and 'livelock' both feel wrong at first — but the four deadlock conditions are satisfied with pool workers as the resource: each worker is held while waiting for another, and nothing can preempt it. The queued tasks that would release the waiters can never be dequeued because no worker is free. Livelock would show high CPU and rising retry counts; this shows idle CPU and no progress at all.

mcq.prompt: This function never waits for `second` while holding `first`, so deadlock is ruled out. What can still go wrong?
choices: Deadlock, if the two references name the same mutex object
A data race on the guarded pair, because try_to_lock does not synchronize
Priority inversion, because a try-lock cannot participate in priority inheritance
Livelock — opposing callers can release and retry in lockstep forever, burning CPU without completing
mcq.explain: Breaking hold-and-wait removes the wait cycle, so no thread is blocked — but two callers arriving in opposite orders can each grab their first mutex, fail the try-lock, release, yield, and repeat indefinitely. That is livelock: the threads execute and react to each other while no operation completes, showing high CPU and a rising retry count rather than blocked stacks. Randomized backoff makes the lockstep unlikely, but it is a contention policy, not a substitute for a coherent lock order. (The same-mutex case is real, which is why the full version in the chapter special-cases `&first == &second` before the loop.)

mcq.prompt: Why is notifying a condition variable *after* releasing its mutex the usual latency optimization?
choices: Because calling notify_one() while holding the mutex is undefined behaviour
Because a waiter woken while the notifier still holds the mutex wakes directly into a blocked acquire of that same mutex
Because notify_one() cannot be called from a thread that owns the associated mutex
Because the predicate state is not visible to other threads until the mutex is released
mcq.explain: Notifying under the lock is perfectly correct — nothing is undefined and nothing forbids it. It is just wasteful: the woken thread's very first action inside wait() is to reacquire the mutex, which the notifier still holds, so it pays a scheduler round trip only to park again. The visibility answer is the subtle wrong one: publishing the predicate state *under* the mutex is what makes it visible to any future lock holder, and that requirement is unchanged by where the notify goes.

reading.explain: 50, deterministically, because the shutdown policy is drain rather than discard. Three rules have to hold at once for that. The `jthread` member is declared last, so it is destroyed first and joins while the mutex, condition variable and queue it uses are still alive. Its destructor requests stop *before* joining, otherwise the destructor would block against a worker that only exits on a stop request. And the stop-aware `condition_variable_any` wait returns when the token is signalled, at which point the worker still checks the queue and only returns once it is empty — so every submitted job is processed. Change that check to `return;` immediately after the wait and the printed number becomes an arbitrary partial count.

reading.section: Data Races and the Mutex Family
reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: Sharding a hot counter is the right instinct, but a `std::vector` is the wrong home for the shards. `std::mutex` is neither copyable nor movable, so `Shard` is neither, and every vector operation that may relocate elements — `reserve`, `emplace_back`, growth — requires the element type to be move-insertable. libc++ reports it as a static assertion, `Cpp17MoveInsertable`, deep inside `__swap_out_circular_buffer`. Note what does compile: `std::vector<Shard> shards(4);` constructs the elements in place and never relocates them. The honest fix for a fixed shard count is `std::array<Shard, 4>`, which states that the addresses are stable — something the shards' users are implicitly relying on anyway.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: std::ref made the argument storable and preserved reference semantics, but it did not extend anything's lifetime. The unique_ptr frees the int at the end of the inner scope, and the semaphore then deliberately releases the worker so it dereferences the freed object — AddressSanitizer reports 'heap-use-after-free ... READ of size 4'. Note that the join is correct and comes too late to help: joining guarantees the worker has finished, not that what it referred to was still alive while it ran.

reading.section: Data Races and the Mutex Family
reading.explain: `100 0` every time. Four hundred attempts chase one hundred permits and the count can never go negative, because the check and the decrement are one transaction: they happen under the same lock acquisition, so no thread can observe `available_ > 0` and then have another thread consume the last permit before it decrements. That is precisely what the `std::atomic<int> available` version cannot promise — every individual access there is race-free, and the compound decision still is not, which is a race condition without a data race. Note also that `available()` locks even though it only reads: locking the writers and leaving the reader unlocked would still be a data race, and `mutable` on the mutex is what lets a const accessor do it.

reading.section: Data Races and the Mutex Family
reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The comment is the bug. A data race needs two conflicting accesses with no happens-before edge, and only one of them has to be a write — the reader being read-only does not exempt it. The writer holds `progress_mutex` for every store, the reader holds nothing, so no edge exists and the program has undefined behaviour, not merely a chance of a stale percentage. The consequence is worse than a wrong number: the compiler may hoist the load of `percent_done` out of the reader's loop entirely, because it is entitled to assume no race occurs. Every access to guarded state must follow the same policy — the reader must take the lock, or `percent_done` must become a `std::atomic<int>` and stop being mutex-guarded at all. ASan and UBSan do not instrument for races, so a quiet run here is expected; ThreadSanitizer is the tool that reports it.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The stop-token overload of `wait` belongs to `std::condition_variable_any`, not to `std::condition_variable`; clang reports "no matching member function for call to 'wait'" and offers only the two-argument predicate form. The distinction is not bureaucratic. `condition_variable` is specialised for `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>` so it can hand that one mutex to the platform's wait primitive; the stop-token overload has to install a `stop_callback` that notifies the variable, which needs the generality (and the extra internal mutex) that `condition_variable_any` carries. Changing the declaration to `std::condition_variable_any` is the whole fix — and it matters, because a worker parked on a plain `condition_variable` sleeps straight through a stop request unless someone wires up the wake by hand.

`4 10`, and it does not depend on whether the consumer or the producer runs first. The predicate is a disjunction of two pieces of durable state — 'there is a value' or 'the channel is closed' — so a consumer that arrives before anything is sent parks and is woken, and a consumer that arrives after the channel has already been closed and drained returns `nullopt` without parking at all. The ordering inside `receive()` is the part worth copying: it tests emptiness *after* the wait rather than testing `closed_` first. Reversing those two — `if (closed_) return std::nullopt;` before draining — would silently discard values that were sent before the close, which is the classic way a shutdown path loses the last few messages. `close()` uses `notify_all` because one state change enables every waiter at once, and `send()` uses `notify_one` because one value satisfies exactly one consumer.

`3 2`. A `std::once_flag` is completed only when its callable returns normally, so the first two attempts throw, propagate to their own caller, and leave the flag unset — which is exactly what makes retrying possible. The third attempt returns normally, completes the flag, and calls four and five do nothing at all. That retry semantics is the reason to prefer `call_once` over the hand-rolled `if (!done) { init(); done = true; }`: written that way with `done` set first, a throwing initialiser would permanently mark a half-initialised object as ready. Note the obligation that comes with the feature — a retryable initialiser must be safe to run twice, so it must not leave partially assigned members behind when it throws.

reading.section: The C++20 Kit: Semaphores, Latches, Barriers, and Atomic Wait
reading.explain: `3 6`. The completion function runs exactly once per phase — not once per arrival — on one of the participating threads, after the last participant arrives and before any of them is released. Three phases therefore give three completions, and the last one observes all six increments because every partition performs its `fetch_add` before its `arrive_and_wait`. That is the property a barrier sells: the completion step sees the phase's work finished and nobody sees phase N+1 begin before it. A latch could not express this at all, because it is one-shot and cannot reset. The protocol obligation is the flip side: every remaining participant must reach every phase, so a partition that returned early — or threw — would leave its peer waiting forever unless it used `arrive_and_drop()`.

There are five instances of local_count — one per worker plus one for the main thread. Each worker increments only its own to 3 with plain, unsynchronized operations (thread confinement removes the need for a lock), then publishes its subtotal once, giving 4 x 3 = 12. The main thread's instance was never touched by any worker, so it still reads 0. That last value is the whole point: `thread_local` is not a shared variable with a fancy name.

writing.prompt: Write a MarketFeed class that starts one background worker in its constructor. The worker must never observe a member that has not been constructed yet; shutdown must be correct on ordinary scope exit and during exception unwinding without the caller ever calling join(); and a stop requested before the worker's first iteration must still end it. Add comments stating what fixes both orderings.
checklist: The std::jthread member is declared last, after every member the worker touches
A comment states that members are constructed in declaration order, so declaring the worker last means it starts only after the state it uses exists
A comment states that members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, so the worker joins while that state is still alive
The callable takes a std::stop_token and tests stop_requested() at the top of the loop, before doing work
Shared state is guarded by a mutex (or is atomic), including in any const accessor
No explicit join(), detach(), or destructor is written
writing.notes: No destructor is written and none should be: `jthread` already implements request-stop-then-join, and writing `~MarketFeed() { worker_.join(); }` would deadlock against a worker that only exits on a stop request. Note the limit of the guarantee — the request takes effect only when the worker reaches a check, so a `poll_once()` that can block indefinitely makes `~MarketFeed` block indefinitely too. The answer to that is a wakeable wait, not `detach()`.

writing.prompt: A pricing worker records a hit or a miss for every quote it processes, millions of times per second, and a monitoring thread wants a process-wide total once a second. Write it so the hot path performs no lock and no atomic read-modify-write, and publication to the shared totals happens at an explicit boundary you choose. Comment on the two costs the chapter attributes to thread_local and on why the counters must not be keyed to a logical request.
checklist: The per-thread counters are thread_local and updated with plain, unsynchronized increments
The shared totals are atomic and are touched only at the publication boundary, not per event
Publication is explicit (a flush function or an RAII object), not a side effect of every record
A comment names the per-thread guard check on a dynamically initialized thread-local
A comment names the footprint multiplication by the number of participating threads
A comment states that a task resumed on another pool worker sees that worker's instance, so request-scoped data does not belong here
writing.notes: The hot path is now a plain increment of a thread-local struct — no lock, no atomic, no shared cache line to bounce — and the cost of that is that a reader of the totals is always looking at a slightly old picture. That is the batching trade in its purest form. If the flush interval matters, publish from the worker's own loop at a natural boundary rather than letting the monitoring thread reach into another thread's storage, which it cannot safely do.

writing.prompt: One mutex-protected counter updated by every worker forms a lock convoy. Write a sharded replacement: a fixed number of independently locked shards, an add() that touches exactly one shard, and a total(). State total()'s semantics in a comment, and explain in a comment why the shards cannot live in a std::vector.
checklist: A fixed-size std::array of shards, each with its own mutex and its own subtotal
A comment states that std::mutex is neither copyable nor movable, so a std::vector of shards cannot reserve, grow, or relocate
Shards are padded or aligned so two shards do not share a cache line
add() acquires exactly one shard's mutex, chosen from the caller's identity or a supplied index
total() acquires each shard in turn and a comment states that the sum is a snapshot, not a value that stays true
A comment names what sharding costs: readers now pay N acquisitions instead of one
writing.notes: The design trades write scalability for read cost: writers now contend eight ways instead of one, and every reader pays eight acquisitions. That is the right trade for a counter written constantly and read once a second, and the wrong one for a value read in a hot loop. Choose `shard_hint` from something stable and cheap — a worker index handed out at startup beats hashing a thread id on every call, and it also keeps a given worker on a line it already owns.

writing.section: RAII Lock Wrappers and Multi-Lock Deadlock Avoidance
writing.prompt: Write `rebalance(Book& from, Book& to, int lots, const std::function<void(int)>& on_moved)` where each Book owns a mutex guarding its own inventory. It must be deadlock-free when two threads rebalance in opposite directions, correct when from and to name the same book, and it must invoke the callback with no mutex held. Comment on why the callback placement is a correctness requirement and not a style preference.
checklist: Uses std::scoped_lock for the two mutexes rather than two sequential locks
Special-cases &from == &to before locking, since locking one std::mutex twice is undefined
The sufficiency check and both updates happen inside one critical section
Anything the callback needs is copied into locals before the lock is released
The callback is invoked after the critical section ends
A comment states that calling unknown code under a mutex imports that code's lock acquisitions into this function's lock order
writing.notes: The pairwise invariant is that a completed rebalance preserves total inventory across the two books, which is why the check and both updates must sit inside one critical section — releasing between them would expose a state where the lots exist in neither book. Note the asymmetry the callback creates: because it runs unlocked, `remaining` is a value that was true at the moment of the move and may already be stale when the callback reads it. Say so in the callback's contract rather than letting a caller assume otherwise.

writing.prompt: Write a RouteTable whose pick(hash) is called concurrently from many threads and whose install(backends) replaces the whole set rarely. Then add retire_backend(id), which discovers under a shared lock that it must modify the table. Show what it must do — a shared lock cannot be upgraded — and comment on both the deadlock that upgrading would cause and the measurement that would justify shared_mutex here at all.
checklist: Readers use std::shared_lock, writers use std::unique_lock, and the std::shared_mutex member is mutable
install() takes its container by value and moves it into place under the exclusive lock
retire_backend() releases the shared lock before taking the exclusive lock
After taking the exclusive lock it re-checks the condition, because the table may have changed in between
A comment states that there is no upgrade operation and that two readers each waiting to upgrade would deadlock
A comment states that read duration, not read percentage, is what justifies shared_mutex over a plain mutex
writing.notes: The drop-recheck-act shape is the general answer whenever a reader discovers it must write, and the re-check is the whole point: the observation that motivated the upgrade was made under a lock that has since been released, so it is a hint, not a fact. If that pattern turns out to be the common path rather than the rare one, the reader-writer lock is buying nothing and a plain `std::mutex` — or an immutable table published by pointer swap — is the simpler design.

writing.prompt: Write a bounded blocking queue with push() and pop(). A push into a full queue must wait for space; a pop from an empty queue must wait for an item. Use two condition variables and explain in a comment why one is not enough.
checklist: Separate not_empty and not_full condition variables, each with its own predicate
Both predicates describe durable state (size, emptiness), not an event
Waits use std::unique_lock and the predicate overload, never a bare wait()
Predicate state is only read and modified while the mutex is held
Each operation notifies the *other* condition variable after changing state
A comment explains that one shared CV would wake producers for consumer events and vice versa
writing.notes: Both predicates describe state — 'the queue is nonempty', 'the queue has room' — which is what makes them survive scheduling delay and spurious wakeups. A predicate phrased as 'a notification occurred' cannot, because condition variables store no signals. The bound is also a design decision, not just a number: it is where the system chooses to block producers instead of converting overload into unbounded memory growth.

writing.prompt: Reference data must be loaded exactly once per symbol, however many threads ask for the same symbol concurrently, and a load that throws must be retryable by a later caller. Write it. Say in comments why the flags cannot live directly in an unordered_map's mapped type, and what must not go inside the once callable.
checklist: One std::once_flag per symbol, with std::call_once, rather than one flag for the whole table
The entries are held by stable address (node handles, unique_ptr, or a node-based container), since a once_flag is neither copyable nor movable and rehashing must not move it
The table's own mutex is released before call_once runs, so loading one symbol does not block lookups of another
A comment states that a throwing loader leaves that symbol's flag unset, so a later call retries
A comment states that only the initialization belongs inside the callable
The loaded data is only read after call_once returns
writing.notes: Two different one-time problems are nested here and they need different mechanisms: 'does an entry for this symbol exist yet' is a short mutation of a shared container and belongs under a mutex, while 'has this symbol's data been loaded' is a potentially slow one-shot and belongs to a `once_flag`. Collapsing them into one mutex held across the load would serialise every symbol behind the slowest one. Note also what `call_once` still does not give you: there is no reset, so a symbol whose reference data must be reloaded needs an explicit version, not a recycled flag.

writing.section: The C++20 Kit: Semaphores, Latches, Barriers, and Atomic Wait
writing.prompt: A service must not accept traffic until every subsystem has reported ready, and a subsystem whose startup throws must not leave the gate closed forever. Write the startup sequence and the coordinator's wait. Comment on why a latch is the right primitive and on what you would use instead if the subsystems had to rendezvous at the end of every phase.
checklist: std::latch constructed with the subsystem count
Every subsystem counts down on every path, including the throwing path — an RAII guard or a catch block, not a bare call at the end
A failure is recorded in shared state so the coordinator can distinguish ready from failed
The coordinator waits on the latch and then inspects the failure state before accepting traffic
Workers are std::jthread stored in a container so joining is automatic
A comment states that a latch is one-shot and names std::barrier as the reusable per-phase alternative
writing.notes: The latch answers 'has everyone reported', which is deliberately not the same question as 'did everyone succeed' — mixing the two into one counter is how a startup path ends up either hanging on failure or accepting traffic into a broken subsystem. Keeping them separate costs one atomic and makes both outcomes explicit. Note that `count_down()` and `wait()` are the two halves a latch offers separately; `arrive_and_wait()` is for participants that are also waiting, which the coordinator here is not.

writing.prompt: Write submit() and the worker loop for a fixed pool whose task queue is bounded. Contract: submit() must never block and never grow the queue — it returns false when full; close() must be safe to call twice and must wake every parked worker; a worker must exit only once the queue is drained; and no task may run with the queue mutex held. State the shutdown policy and the overload policy in comments.
checklist: The queue has a capacity and submit() returns false rather than waiting or growing
close() sets durable state under the mutex, notifies all workers, and is idempotent
The wait predicate is a statement about state: a task exists, or the pool is closed
The exit condition requires both closed and an empty queue, so queued work still runs
The task is moved out of the queue into a local and invoked after the lock is released
Comments state the shutdown policy (drain, not discard) and the overload policy (reject, not block or grow)
writing.notes: The predicate is a disjunction because two different facts can end the wait, and the exit test that follows it is `tasks_.empty()` rather than `closed_` — checking `closed_` first would discard queued work and quietly change the shutdown policy. Running `task()` outside the lock is not an optimisation either: the mutex's written invariant is 'this guards the queue', and executing arbitrary user code under it would serialise the whole pool and let one slow task block every producer. `std::move_only_function<void()>` is the better element type once your library ships it, since `std::function` forces every task to be copyable.

writing.prompt: A global lock order only helps if it is followed, and the violation is usually on a rare error path that fails in production at 3am. Write a HierarchicalMutex that turns an out-of-order acquisition into an immediate, loud failure on the thread that made the mistake. Contract: each mutex carries a level; a thread may acquire one only if its level is strictly below every level it already holds; the previous level must be restored on unlock, including when the critical section throws; and it must work with std::lock_guard. Name the deadlock condition it enforces and one pathology it does nothing about.
checklist: A thread_local variable records the lowest level the calling thread currently holds, initialized to the maximum
lock() checks the level before acquiring and throws (or aborts) rather than proceeding
The previous level is saved as a member and restored in unlock()
unlock() restores the level, so an exception inside the critical section still restores it through the lock_guard's destructor
The type provides lock(), unlock() and try_lock() so it satisfies the standard mutex requirements
A comment names circular wait as the condition being ruled out and names a pathology it does not address, such as convoying or livelock
writing.notes: The value of this type is not the mutual exclusion, which `std::mutex` already provided; it is that the ordering rule becomes executable and fails on the thread that violated it. Note the design choice of storing `previous_level_` in the mutex rather than in the thread: it works because a correctly nested critical section unlocks in reverse order, and it is exactly why recursive acquisition of the same `HierarchicalMutex` is rejected — `level_ >= current_level` — which is a feature rather than an omission. Assigning levels is the real work, and it must cover error paths, teardown, and anything a callback may reach.
